posts.t:
Here is a setup that looked good, but there was a F/O that I would not have expected if I was live trading. I can't figure out why price blew through the origin. Since the files are large, I have included the full chart zoomed out along with three separate charts that show the close up view of price action.

The trade setup ended up working well- price dropped off as expected and hit its target. What was unexpected, was price faking out above the origin of the important engulf. Is there a way I could have predicted this occurrence?

Could the reason for the F/O be to catch the extreme orders on the RBD to the left of the RBD that the origin of the engulf is reacting to? See chart below... this is my only possible explanation for why this happened. If I am correct in my thinking, is this something we always need to be aware of when trading an engulf like this? Should we always be looking for the extreme set of orders in the FTR/Supply.Demand level to the left of the RBD or DBR for a possible fakeout?
posts.fa:

posts.t:
After thinking more about this fakeout, I remember my writings back on Post #3 when I said:

"IF’s trades often occur at levels where he experiences very little (if any) drawdown. After breaking down some of those amazing trades I notice many times he is able to predict in advance and place a PO at the exact area where price turns.

I could be wrong, but it seems like he knows where the fakeouts will occur by looking left of the engulf to see what the RBD/ DBR (supply/demand) is reacting to (usually an important FTR) and determining whether there are any extreme orders left to fill in that FTR. If so, price will likely FO to a specific decision point within this FTR. That is why he often drop down to a 5 minute or 1 minute chart to plot his entry….he is looking for the most accurate decision point."

Is there a connection to that statement and my last trading example on Post #104?

Hmmm....

posts.t: Hey, those are stacked zones. The first one ist the origin of the engulf and the second one is the higher RBD to the left. I've already experienced myself. Many times price will fake out to the zone that is directly above or below the zone you want to trade.. Watch it! You will see this often! For me there are three possible actions: 1) Leave it be 2) If you really want to get in: Entry at first and Sl behind second zone. Problem: R:R gets worse 3) Anticipate the Fakout, entry and Sl at second zone. If price hits your PO, great! If not, nevermind. I like to use the last one, R:R is better and if I can't get in, then I look for another setup. We don't have to chase them In the last post in my journal I had the same problem ( only with stacked supply). I will enter lower then the origin so I don't get faked out... Regards!

posts.t:
Thanks Harsh and TTF - The true supply makes sense, and I think it is the same idea as price moving to collect remaining orders.

Here is my dilemma: the area where price faked out on Post # 104 is also a failed QM. So would we identify this as a diamond formation as well? If so, there following would all be true about this example, right?

1. It was a F/O to true supply/extreme orders 2. Diamond Formation 3. Stacked orders zone

If all three of these are true, how can we possible trade without leaving a stop loss way too high above the entry order? That decimates the R:R. TTF had a good idea of placing a P/O in the extreme of the stacked order zone and wait for price to F/O. That's a good idea, but it seems like a lot of phenomenal trades could be missed. Is there any other way we might be able to predict this diamond formation?

And last question: what defines a stacked order? Is there a rule of thumb for identifying stacked orders (such as how far the orders are from each other, how many are in a specified area etc...?) Because if you look hard enough there are always going to be supply/demand zones above/below your entries. is the determination of whether they are 'stacked' simply depended on how close they are to your entry?

Thanks for your inputs everyone!

posts.t:
Here is a chart I just marked up USD-CAD. This was a failed setup.

Lately I have had a lot of help from RTM traders and my understanding has taken a major step forward. It never occurred to me that the best engulf is an engulf of an FTR that previously engulfed an important zone.

My next question: suppose there is a perfect setup occurring (like the USD/CAD example below...I drew a red arrow pointing to the area where I saw an engulf of an important FTR). If I was trading this chart live, I would be preparing to take a short once price moved back to the origin of the engulf. Only in this example, price blows right through the origin of the engulf and goes on to make major new highs. In this case, I would assume what was labeled as an 'engulf' of the 'important FTR' was really a F/O.

Would you agree this was the reason for the failed USD/CAD setup?

Here is a close-up
posts.fa:
اینجا چارتی است که تازه علامت زدم روی USD-CAD. این یک ستاپ شکست‌خورده بود.

اخیراً کمک زیادی از معامله‌گران RTM گرفتم و درکم یک گام بزرگ به جلو برداشته. هرگز به ذهنم نرسیده بود که بهترین اینگالف، اینگالفی است که یک FTR را اینگالف می‌کند که قبلاً ناحیه‌ای مهم را اینگالف کرده بود.

سؤال بعدی من: فرض کن یک ستاپ کامل در حال رخ‌دادن است (مثل مثال USD/CAD پایین… یک پیکان قرمز کشیدم که به ناحیه‌ای اشاره می‌کند که در آن اینگالفی از یک FTR مهم دیدم). اگر این چارت را زنده معامله می‌کردم، آماده می‌شدم که وقتی قیمت به مبدأ اینگالف برگشت فروش بگیرم. فقط در این مثال، قیمت مستقیم از مبدأ اینگالف رد می‌شود و سقف‌های جدید بزرگی می‌سازد. در این حالت، فرض می‌کنم چیزی که به‌عنوان 'اینگالف' 'FTR مهم' علامت خورده در واقع یک F/O بوده.

آیا موافقی که این دلیل ستاپ شکست‌خوردهٔ USD/CAD بود؟

این یک نمای نزدیک است

posts.t:
A quick observation about stacked zones: I think the difference between stacked zones and compression is stacked zones have valid orders untouched by price on FTB. Compression is basically stacked zones which have already been taken out (consumed) by price revisiting the levels.

At least I think that's correct...

posts.t:
The following are drawings I made to illustrate some additional questions I have:

Example 1:

In this example, a Flag limit has broke an S/R level but there isn't a retrace after the break to form a FTR. Is this Flag still relevant and important? I would say yes, because the decision point within the flag is the origin of price breaking the S/R level. Would a future engulf of this Flag be as important as an engulf of an FTR?

Example 2:

Like in example 1, the decision point within the flag exists and it represents the origin of price breaking the S/R. Then, a FTR forms and eventually price visits the FTR on its FTB. Since the FTR retraced back into the flag limit however, is the FTR also the FTB to the original Flag Limit? In this example, does the DP within the flag limit hold more significance with regard to a future engulf, or does the FTR hold more significance with regard to a future engulf?

Example 3:

I see this occur quite often. A flag breaks through a S/R level and price technically forms an FTR, but price doesn't take off for long. It quickly retraces back to the original flag after posting a brief new high/new low (which is required for an FTR to be valid). In this case, would the weak FTR formed hold more significance with regard to a future engulf, or does the original flag (which hold the original decision point to break the S/R level) be more significant with regard to a future engulf?

Here is an engulf setup, which is valid:

Is the following diagram also valid? In this example, there is only a Flag limit (no FTR formed after the break of the S/R level). There is only a small hiccup DBD that occurs after the break. Is the engulf scenario still valid and can it be traded in the same way?

موارد زیر نقاشی‌هایی هستند که برای نشان‌دادن چند سؤال اضافی‌ام کشیدم:

مثال 1:

در این مثال، یک حد فلگ یک سطح S/R را شکسته اما بازگشتی پس از شکست برای تشکیل FTR نیست. آیا این فلگ هنوز مرتبط و مهم است؟ می‌گویم بله، چون نقطهٔ تصمیم‌گیری درون فلگ مبدأ شکست قیمتِ سطح S/R است. آیا یک اینگالف آینده از این فلگ به‌اندازهٔ یک اینگالف از یک FTR مهم خواهد بود؟

مثال 2:

مثل مثال 1، نقطهٔ تصمیم‌گیری درون فلگ وجود دارد و مبدأ شکست قیمتِ S/R را نشان می‌دهد. بعد، یک FTR شکل می‌گیرد و در نهایت قیمت FTR را در FTB خود بازدید می‌کند. با این حال چون FTR به داخل حد فلگ برگشته، آیا FTR هم FTB به FL اصلی است؟ در این مثال، آیا DP درون حد فلگ از نظر اینگالف آینده اهمیت بیشتری دارد، یا FTR از نظر اینگالف آینده اهمیت بیشتری دارد؟

مثال 3:

این را خیلی اغلب می‌بینم. یک فلگ از میان یک سطح S/R عبور می‌کند و قیمت از نظر فنی یک FTR می‌سازد، اما قیمت مدت زیادی جهش نمی‌کند. سریع به فلگ اصلی برمی‌گردد پس از ثبت یک سقف/کف جدید کوتاه (که برای معتبر بودن یک FTR لازم است). در این حالت، آیا FTR ضعیفِ شکل‌گرفته از نظر اینگالف آینده اهمیت بیشتری دارد، یا فلگ اصلی (که نقطهٔ تصمیم‌گیری اصلی برای شکست سطح S/R را دارد) از نظر اینگالف آینده معنادارتر است؟

اینجا یک ستاپ اینگالف است که معتبر است:

آیا دیاگرام زیر هم معتبر است؟ در این مثال، فقط یک حد فلگ وجود دارد (پس از شکست سطح S/R هیچ FTR‌ی شکل نگرفته). فقط یک اختلال کوچک DBD پس از شکست رخ می‌دهد. آیا سناریوی اینگالف هنوز معتبر است و می‌توان آن را به همان شکل معامله کرد؟

posts.t:
H dont get caught out by these setups. You have to take into consideration the context. Engulf or no, price dropped into a really nice SR level. If price moves *between* levels, then price just dropped from supply and hit the floor of the current level. You need to be watching price to flag and give signs of weakness at SR for a sign that it wants to come down into the lower zone. Instead you get a beautiful long setup...the short trade was complete at this level, and if you wanted to see if it broke down some more, you needed to be ready to close. Look at the HTF, you should see if you zoom out why taking the long was worth the trade.

Just my 2 cents.

H این ستاپ‌ها را به دام نیفت. باید زمینه را در نظر بگیری. اینگالف باشد یا نه، قیمت به یک سطح SR واقعاً خوب افت کرد. اگر قیمت *بین* سطوح حرکت کند، پس قیمت فقط از عرضه افت کرد و به کف سطح فعلی خورد. باید قیمت را زیر نظر داشته باشی که در SR فلگ بسازد و نشانه‌های ضعف بدهد که می‌خواهد به ناحیهٔ پایین‌تر بیاید. در عوض یک ستاپ خرید زیبا می‌گیری… معاملهٔ فروش در همین سطح کامل شده بود و اگر می‌خواستی ببینی بیشتر می‌شکند یا نه، باید آمادهٔ بستن می‌شدی. به HTF نگاه کن، باید ببینی اگر زوم کنی چرا خرید گرفتن ارزش معامله را داشت.

posts.t:
Hi PTP,

What do you think of this diagram? (I found it over on IF's journal, and I think CharliePips created it)

It appears (from RTM philosophy) that when an FTR the breaks a significant S/R level occurs and is itself engulfed, a new FTR is formed which is highly important. When price reacts to this highly important FTR it often originates a trade able engulf (not always though, and sometimes it is a fakeout).

They say that all of this needs to occur at a major S/R flip level.

I have found some really nice examples of this working, and to some degree i seems to coincide with your previous advice of focusing first on S/R levels to look for reactions. Have you found that this is a good price action setup, or have you found it doesn't work well?

Many thanks!
posts.fa:
سلام PTP،

نظرت دربارهٔ این دیاگرام چیست؟ (آن را در ژورنال IF پیدا کردم و فکر می‌کنم CharliePips آن را ساخته)

به‌نظر می‌رسد (از فلسفهٔ RTM) وقتی یک FTR که یک سطح S/R معنادار را می‌شکند رخ می‌دهد و خودش اینگالف می‌شود، یک FTR جدید شکل می‌گیرد که بسیار مهم است. وقتی قیمت به این FTR بسیار مهم واکنش نشان می‌دهد اغلب یک اینگالف قابل‌معامله را آغاز می‌کند (هرچند همیشه نه، و گاهی یک فیک‌اوت است).

می‌گویند همهٔ این‌ها باید در یک سطح سواپ بزرگ S/R رخ دهد.

نمونه‌های واقعاً خوبی از کارکردن این پیدا کرده‌ام و تا حدی با توصیهٔ قبلی تو دربارهٔ تمرکز اول روی سطوح S/R برای جست‌وجوی واکنش‌ها هم‌خوانی دارد. آیا دریافت که این یک ستاپ price action خوب است، یا دریافت که خوب کار نمی‌کند؟

سپاس بسیار!
